founding_context: Created after the June 1977 legislative elections, in which candidates running as 'independents' won a majority of seats. Ahmed Osman, prime minister from 1972 to 1977 and brother-in-law of King Hassan II, gathered dozens of these independent MPs and business and political figures into a party in 1978. The party was widely read as a palace-aligned ('administrative') formation designed to give the pro-monarchy majority a partisan structure.

timeline.title: Independents win the 1977 legislative elections
timeline.description: Candidates running without party label ('indépendants') obtained the largest bloc in the 1977 House of Representatives, forming the base from which the RNI was later built.

timeline.title: Founding of the RNI
timeline.description: Former prime minister Ahmed Osman founds the Rassemblement national des indépendants from the independent MPs' group. French Wikipedia gives 6 October 1978; Arabic Wikipedia gives 28 November 1978 as the founding congress date.

timeline.title: Split: dissident MPs form the Parti national démocrate
timeline.description: A group of RNI parliamentarians led by Mohamed Arsalane El Jadidi broke away and created the Parti national démocrate (PND). (General knowledge; not re-verified in this session — see notes file.)

timeline.title: Joins the Youssoufi 'alternance' government
timeline.description: The RNI took part in the government of Abderrahmane Youssoufi (USFP) alongside the Koutla parties. (General knowledge; ministerial count not sourced in this session.)

timeline.title: Osman removed; Mustapha Mansouri elected president
timeline.description: After Ahmed Osman was pushed out in April 2007, a congress on 21-23 May 2007 elected Mustapha Mansouri, then minister of employment, as party president.

timeline.title: Enters the Abbas El Fassi government
timeline.description: After the September 2007 elections the RNI joined the Istiqlal-led government; Salaheddine Mezouar became Minister of Economy and Finance and Aziz Akhannouch Minister of Agriculture (Akhannouch was then without party label and joined the RNI later). (General knowledge; ministerial count not sourced.)

timeline.title: Salaheddine Mezouar elected president
timeline.description: At a congress in Marrakech, Salaheddine Mezouar was elected president of the RNI, replacing Mustapha Mansouri.

timeline.title: 2011 legislative elections: third place, goes into opposition
timeline.description: The RNI won 52 seats (general knowledge figure) behind the PJD and Istiqlal and sat in opposition to the Benkirane I government.

timeline.title: Enters the Benkirane II government with 8 ministries
timeline.description: After Istiqlal's withdrawal, the RNI negotiated its entry into a reshuffled coalition. It obtained eight ministries including Foreign Affairs (Mezouar), Economy and Finance (Boussaid), Agriculture (Akhannouch) and Industry (Elalamy).

timeline.title: 2016 legislative elections: 37 seats
timeline.description: The RNI fell to 37 seats (fourth place). Its state subsidy consequently fell from about 6.7 MDH to 5.4 MDH per year from 2017.

timeline.title: Aziz Akhannouch elected president
timeline.description: Following Mezouar's resignation, Aziz Akhannouch, Minister of Agriculture and one of Morocco's wealthiest businessmen, was elected RNI president at an extraordinary congress.

timeline.title: The 'blocage': five-month government-formation deadlock ends with Benkirane's dismissal
timeline.description: After the October 2016 elections, PJD leader Abdelilah Benkirane could not form a government because Akhannouch first demanded Istiqlal's exclusion (achieved after Chabat's remarks on Mauritania) and then the inclusion of the USFP and UC, which Benkirane refused. On 15 March 2017 the King relieved Benkirane and appointed Saâdeddine El Othmani, who accepted the RNI's conditions.

timeline.title: Seven portfolios in the El Othmani government
timeline.description: The RNI negotiated seven portfolios, including Economy and Finance, Agriculture and Fisheries, Justice, and Industry and Investment.

timeline.title: Consumer boycott targets Afriquia
timeline.description: A social-media boycott campaign targeted Centrale Danone, Sidi Ali and Afriquia, the fuel distributor owned by Akhannouch's Akwa group (about 39% of the fuel market). Within two weeks over 90% of Moroccans were aware of the campaign; it was framed around prices, market concentration and business-politics conflicts of interest.

timeline.title: Wins the 2021 general elections
timeline.description: The RNI came first with 102 of 395 seats in the House of Representatives (+65), 9,995 communal seats, 27 of 120 Chamber of Councillors seats and about 60% of professional-chamber presidencies. It formed a coalition with the PAM and Istiqlal, each taking 4 of the 12 regional presidencies.

timeline.title: Akhannouch government appointed
timeline.description: King Mohammed VI appointed the Akhannouch government: 24 ministers and deputy ministers, 18 from the three coalition parties (RNI 7 portfolios plus the head of government, PAM 7, Istiqlal 4) and 6 without party affiliation; seven women ministers.

timeline.title: Fuel-price surge revives conflict-of-interest accusations
timeline.description: With fuel prices rising after the Ukraine war, opposition parties and the 'Akhannouch dégage' online campaign accused the head of government of profiting through Afriquia; the government refused to reinstate price caps. (Month approximate.)

timeline.title: Competition Council settlement with fuel distributors including Afriquia
timeline.description: The Competition Council concluded a 1.84 billion MAD settlement with nine fuel companies, including Afriquia SMDC (Akwa group), for anti-competitive practices on the diesel and petrol market; the amount was criticised as too low by some observers.

timeline.title: Desalination contract controversy
timeline.description: The PJD accused Akhannouch of conflict of interest after the Casablanca seawater desalination contract was awarded to a consortium including Afriquia Gaz.

timeline.title: Akhannouch II reshuffle
timeline.description: A cabinet reshuffle produced the Akhannouch II government; press reports describe it as more generous in portfolios to the PAM, RNI and Istiqlal. (Exact per-party counts not retrieved in this session.)

timeline.title: GenZ 212 protests demand the government's resignation
timeline.description: From 27 September 2025, youth-led 'GenZ 212' protests over health and education spread across Moroccan cities after the deaths of eight pregnant women at Agadir's public hospital. On 2-3 October the collective called for the government's resignation. The government announced measures on 19 October; protests continued on 25-26 October.

timeline.title: Akhannouch announces he will not seek a third term
timeline.description: Akhannouch announced he would not stand again for the RNI presidency, citing the two-term limit in the party statutes; the announcement, coming after the 2025 protests and the Africa Cup of Nations, took the party by surprise according to Jeune Afrique. He also said he would not stand in the September 2026 legislative elections.

timeline.title: Mohamed Chouki elected president
timeline.description: At an extraordinary congress in El Jadida, Mohamed Chouki, president of the RNI parliamentary group, was elected president as sole candidate after Mohamed Aujjar withdrew.

achievements.title: First place in the 2021 general elections
achievements.description: From 37 seats in 2016 to 102 in 2021, the largest gain of any party, plus first place in communal, regional and professional-chamber elections.
achievements.verification: Confirmed by Ministry of Interior results as reported by Médias24 and others.

achievements.title: Generalisation of compulsory health insurance (AMO)
achievements.description: The RNI-led government claims the extension of AMO to the self-employed and to former RAMED beneficiaries (AMO Tadamon, from December 2022) as its flagship social achievement.
achievements.verification: The generalisation of social protection is a royal project launched by the King in April 2021 under framework law 09-21, adopted before the Akhannouch government took office; the government implemented it. Independent assessments of enrolment and effective access were not retrieved in this session (search budget exhausted).

achievements.title: Direct social aid programme
achievements.description: The government launched direct cash transfers to households (from December 2023), which the RNI presents as delivering the 'social state'.
achievements.verification: Programme exists and was launched in December 2023 (general knowledge); independent evaluation of targeting and the number of beneficiary households was not retrieved in this session.

achievements.title: Financial self-reliance through member contributions
achievements.description: The party's member contributions rose from a low base to 14.5 MDH in 2017 and 16.8 MDH in 2018, making the RNI the second-richest party after the PJD and the least dependent on state subsidy (about 13% of resources).
achievements.verification: Based on Cour des comptes audit data as analysed by Médias24 and Le360; Le360 attributed the growth to Akhannouch's personal wealth pulling in contributions.

Founding date differs between fr.wikipedia (6 Oct 1978) and ar.wikipedia (28 Nov 1978). 1981 split, 1998/2007 government entries, 2002/2007/2011 seat counts and Akhannouch's 29 Oct 2016 election date come from general knowledge and were not re-verified because the WebSearch budget was exhausted. Women MPs 2021 = 16 assumes all RNI women were elected on regional lists (only 6 women won local seats, none RNI). Liberal International membership unverified.

founding_context: In January 2008 Fouad Ali El Himma, a close friend of King Mohammed VI and former minister delegate for the interior, launched the 'Mouvement pour tous les démocrates' with former left-wing activists, human-rights figures and ex-officials. On 7 August 2008 the movement became the PAM through the merger of five small parties (Al Ahd, Alliance des libertés, Parti de l'environnement et du développement, Parti national démocrate, Initiative citoyenne pour le développement). Its stated aim was to revitalise political life and offer an alternative to the rising Islamist PJD; critics labelled it a 'parti administratif' created by the palace.

timeline.title: Launch of the Mouvement pour tous les démocrates
timeline.description: Fouad Ali El Himma, who had resigned as minister delegate for the interior and been elected MP in 2007, launched a movement gathering former leftists, human-rights activists and ex-officials.

timeline.title: Founding of the PAM
timeline.description: Five small parties (Al Ahd, Alliance des libertés, Parti de l'environnement et du développement, Parti national démocrate, Initiative citoyenne pour le développement) merged into the Parti authenticité et modernité, led provisionally by Hassan Benaddi.

timeline.title: First national congress: Biadillah secretary general
timeline.description: The first congress (20-22 February 2009) elected Mohamed Cheikh Biadillah, replacing Hassan Benaddi.

timeline.title: First place in the 2009 communal elections
timeline.description: Less than a year after its creation the PAM came first in the communal elections (general knowledge: about 6,000 seats, roughly 21%), establishing itself as a major local force. (Figures not verified in this session.)

timeline.title: 20 February protests target El Himma and the PAM
timeline.description: Protesters of the 20 February Movement singled out Fouad Ali El Himma and the PAM as symbols of palace interference in politics. El Himma left the party's leadership in 2011 and was named royal adviser in December 2011. (Dates from general knowledge.)

timeline.title: 2011 legislative elections: opposition
timeline.description: The PAM won 47 seats (general knowledge figure) and sat in opposition from 2011 to 2021.

timeline.title: Extraordinary congress: Bakkoury secretary general
timeline.description: At Bouznika (17-19 February 2012), Mustapha Bakkoury was elected with 352 of 388 votes after Biadillah declined to run again; Hakim Benchamach became president of the national council.

timeline.title: First place in communal and regional elections
timeline.description: The PAM came first in the 2015 communal elections with 6,655 seats (21.12%) and, after post-electoral bargaining, won 5 of the 12 regional presidencies (Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima, Oriental, Béni Mellal-Khénifra, Casablanca-Settat, Marrakech-Safi) and 23 Chamber of Councillors seats.

timeline.title: Hakim Benchamach elected President of the House of Councillors
timeline.description: The PAM's Hakim Benchamach became president of the upper house, a post he held until 2021. (Exact date from general knowledge.)

timeline.title: Ilyas El Omari elected secretary general
timeline.description: El Omari, a founder and president of the Tanger-Tétouan-Al Hoceima region, took over from Bakkoury.

timeline.title: 2016 legislative elections: second place with 102 seats
timeline.description: Running an openly anti-PJD campaign, the PAM more than doubled its seats to 102, second behind the PJD (125), but remained in opposition.

timeline.title: El Omari resigns
timeline.description: El Omari resigned as secretary general amid the Rif Hirak crisis in Al Hoceima (in his home region) and one week after a royal speech criticising 'absent' parties. Habib Belkouch handled the interim.

timeline.title: Hakim Benchamach elected secretary general
timeline.description: Benchamach, president of the House of Councillors, was elected to lead the party.

timeline.title: Internal crisis: 'Appel pour l'avenir' current sues the leadership
timeline.description: Thirty-two of the 64 members of the federal bureau demanded an extraordinary national council; on 3 June 2019 the dissident group led by Abdellatif Ouahbi filed a complaint at the Rabat court of first instance to annul Benchamach's 'unilateral decisions'. The crisis included expulsions and lasted until the 2020 congress.

timeline.title: 4th congress: Abdellatif Ouahbi elected
timeline.description: At the 4th national congress in El Jadida (7-9 February 2020), Ouahbi, leader of the 'avenir' current, was elected secretary general, ending the Benchamach era.

timeline.title: 2021 elections: 87 seats, enters government for the first time
timeline.description: The PAM came second with 87 seats (down from 102), won 6,210 communal seats, 19 Councillors seats and 4 regional presidencies, and joined the RNI-led coalition, its first participation in government.

timeline.title: Seven PAM ministers in the Akhannouch government
timeline.description: The PAM obtained seven portfolios, including Justice (Ouahbi), Housing (Mansouri), Youth and Culture (Bensaid), Energy Transition (Benali), Transport (Abdeljalil), Employment (Sekkouri) and Digital Transition (Mezzour).

timeline.title: Lawyers' exam scandal weakens Ouahbi
timeline.description: Allegations of leaks and favouritism in the bar (avocats) entrance exam organised by the Justice ministry triggered protests by candidates and an internal fronde against Ouahbi within the PAM. (Month approximate.)

timeline.title: 'Escobar du Sahara' case: Bioui and Naciri detained
timeline.description: Abdenbi Bioui (president of the Oriental region, MP) and Said Naciri (president of Casablanca prefectural council and Wydad AC), both PAM, were placed in detention in a drug-trafficking and influence-peddling case following the confessions of a Malian trafficker. The party distanced itself from both. Their trial opened on 23 May 2024; the Casablanca court of appeal sentenced Bioui to 12 years and Naciri to 10 years.

timeline.title: 5th congress: collegial leadership under Fatima Zahra Mansouri
timeline.description: The 5th congress in Bouznika (9-11 February 2024) unanimously adopted a three-member collegial general secretariat (Mansouri as coordinator, Bensaid, Abou El Ghali) for four years; Ouahbi did not stand.

timeline.title: Akhannouch II reshuffle
timeline.description: The reshuffle was reported as more generous to the PAM in portfolios. (Per-party counts not retrieved.)

timeline.title: Public rift inside the ruling triumvirate
timeline.description: Le360 reported a 'grosse dispute' in which Salaheddine Abou El Ghali publicly criticised Fatima Zahra Mansouri's management of the party. (Exact date not retrieved.)

timeline.title: 2026 electoral programme: 20 commitments, 350 billion MAD
timeline.description: Ahead of the 23 September 2026 elections the PAM presented a programme of 20 commitments costed at 350 billion MAD. (Month approximate.)

achievements.title: Advanced regionalisation
achievements.description: The party presents itself as the champion of advanced regionalisation and of regional governance, having led 5 of 12 regions after 2015 and 4 after 2021.
achievements.verification: The regionalisation framework (2011 constitution, 2015 organic law 111-14) was a royal/state project prepared by the Consultative Commission on Regionalisation (2010-2011), not a PAM initiative; the PAM's role was in winning regional presidencies. Confirmed: 5 regional presidencies in 2015, 4 in 2021.

achievements.title: Breaking into local government within a year of creation
achievements.description: First place in the 2009 communal elections and in the 2015 communal and regional elections.
achievements.verification: 2015 results confirmed by Ministry of Interior figures (6,655 seats, 21.12%). 2009 figures not verified in this session. Critics attribute the early success to 'transhumance' of notables and administrative support.

achievements.title: Justice reforms under Ouahbi (alternative sentences, criminal-procedure reform)
achievements.description: The PAM claims the law on alternative sentences (43.22) and the reform of the code of criminal procedure as achievements of its Justice minister.
achievements.verification: Law 43.22 on alternative sentences was adopted by parliament in 2024 and entered into force in 2025 (general knowledge; not verified in this session).

achievements.title: Women's representation
achievements.description: First woman to lead a major Moroccan party's executive (Mansouri, 2024); 4 of the 6 women elected in local constituencies in 2021 were PAM.
achievements.verification: The 4-of-6 figure is reported by Le360/Médias24 based on official results.

founding_context: Founded in late 1943 by the core leadership of the banned Parti national (itself heir to the Comité d'action marocaine of 1934), under Allal El Fassi and Ahmed Balafrej. On 11 January 1944 the party published the Manifesto of Independence demanding an end to the French protectorate and a constitutional monarchy under Sultan Mohammed Ben Youssef; the arrests that followed provoked urban unrest. Drawing on the urban bourgeoisie of Fez, Rabat and Salé and on nationalist professionals, it became the dominant nationalist party of the independence struggle.

leaders.name: Ahmed Balafrej
leaders.note: First secretary general; Allal El Fassi was the party's president/za'im from the start. Balafrej was prime minister in 1958 and left the secretariat general in 1960 (month approximate).

leaders.name: Allal El Fassi
leaders.note: Party leader (president) from 1944; took over the secretariat general from Balafrej in 1960 and led the party until his death on 13 May 1974. Hespress mistakenly gives 1972 as year of death.

leaders.name: M'hamed Boucetta
leaders.note: Secretary general after Allal El Fassi's death; Minister of Foreign Affairs 1977-1983; resigned in February 1998.

leaders.name: Abbas El Fassi
leaders.note: Secretary general February 1998 to 23 September 2012; Prime Minister 2007-2011.

leaders.name: Hamid Chabat
leaders.note: Mayor of Fez and UGTM union leader; elected 23 September 2012 with 478 votes against 458 for Abdelouahed El Fassi after the 16th congress (June 2012) postponed the vote. Withdrew the party from government in 2013; his December 2016 remarks on Mauritania cost the party its place in the Benkirane majority talks.

leaders.name: Nizar Baraka
leaders.note: Grandson of Allal El Fassi; elected at the 17th congress (7 October 2017 — date from general knowledge, not re-verified) and re-elected unanimously at the 18th congress in Bouznika on 28 April 2024 after Rachid Afilal withdrew. Minister of Equipment and Water since 2021.

timeline.title: Predecessor: the Parti national
timeline.description: After the 1934 Comité d'action marocaine was dissolved, Allal El Fassi's wing formed the Parti national in 1937, which was banned; its cadres founded the Istiqlal in 1943.

timeline.title: Founding of the Istiqlal Party
timeline.description: Founded by the core leadership of the banned Parti national under Ahmed Balafrej and Allal El Fassi (then in exile in Gabon). Encyclopedia.com and Wikipedia give 1943; the party itself dates its birth to the Manifesto of 11 January 1944.

timeline.title: Manifesto of Independence
timeline.description: The party's charter demanded independence and a constitutional monarchy under the Sultan. The arrest of Balafrej and other signatories triggered serious urban unrest in January-February 1944. The date is now a national holiday.

timeline.title: Independence; Istiqlal dominates the first governments
timeline.description: After independence the Istiqlal held most portfolios in the Bekkai governments and Balafrej became prime minister in May 1958. (General knowledge.)

timeline.title: Split: the left wing founds the UNFP
timeline.description: Mehdi Ben Barka, Prime Minister Abdallah Ibrahim, Abderrahim Bouabid, Mahjoub Ben Seddik and Mohamed Basri left to create the Union nationale des forces populaires, taking much of the party's trade-union and radical base.

timeline.title: Allal El Fassi takes over the secretariat general
timeline.description: Balafrej stepped down and Allal El Fassi combined the presidency and the secretariat general.

timeline.title: Move into opposition
timeline.description: After the 1963 elections and the creation of the pro-palace FDIC, the Istiqlal left government and remained in opposition (with the 1970 Koutla alliance with the UNFP) until 1977.

timeline.title: Death of Allal El Fassi; Boucetta becomes secretary general
timeline.description: Allal El Fassi died in Bucharest on 13 May 1974; M'hamed Boucetta took over the secretariat general.

timeline.title: Return to government
timeline.description: In the context of national consensus on the Western Sahara, Istiqlal leaders were co-opted into the government in 1977; Boucetta became Minister of Foreign Affairs (1977-1983).

timeline.title: Back to opposition after the 1984 elections
timeline.description: Following the 1984 legislative elections the Istiqlal returned to the opposition; in 1992 it co-founded the Koutla démocratique with the USFP, PPS and OADP. (Koutla date from general knowledge.)

timeline.title: Abbas El Fassi elected; party joins the 'alternance' government
timeline.description: Boucetta resigned in February 1998 and Abbas El Fassi became secretary general; the Istiqlal joined Abderrahmane Youssoufi's government in March 1998 and remained in the Jettou governments (2002-2007).

timeline.title: First place in the 2007 legislative elections; Abbas El Fassi prime minister
timeline.description: With 52 seats the Istiqlal became the largest party; Abbas El Fassi was appointed prime minister (government formed 15 October 2007).

timeline.title: Second place with 60 seats; joins the Benkirane I government
timeline.description: Behind the PJD (107), the Istiqlal won 60 seats and entered the Benkirane I government (3 January 2012) with six ministers, including Nizar Baraka at Economy and Finance.

timeline.title: Hamid Chabat elected secretary general
timeline.description: After the 16th congress postponed the vote, Chabat beat Abdelouahed El Fassi 478-458 on 23 September 2012, ending the Fassi family's hold on the leadership.

timeline.title: Withdrawal from the Benkirane government
timeline.description: After months of attacks by Chabat on the government's record (national council decision in May 2013), five of the six Istiqlal ministers (Baraka, Douiri, Amrani, Maâzouz, Kayouh) resigned on 9 July 2013; Mohamed El Ouafa refused and stayed. The government lost its majority until the RNI joined on 10 October 2013.

timeline.title: 2015 local elections: second in communal seats, first in the Chamber of Councillors
timeline.description: The Istiqlal won 5,106 communal seats (16.22%), the presidencies of the two Saharan regions (Laâyoune-Sakia El Hamra, Dakhla-Oued Ed-Dahab) and 24 Councillors seats, the largest group in the upper house.

timeline.title: 2016 legislative elections: 46 seats
timeline.description: The party fell to 46 seats (third place).

timeline.title: Chabat's Mauritania remarks exclude the party from the majority
timeline.description: Chabat's statement describing Mauritania as historically Moroccan land caused a diplomatic incident; Akhannouch used it to demand the Istiqlal's exclusion from Benkirane's coalition talks, which Benkirane conceded in January 2017.

timeline.title: 17th congress: Nizar Baraka elected
timeline.description: After a turbulent congress process in which Chabat said he would 'never abandon' the leadership and clashes pitted his supporters against the Ould Errachid clan, Nizar Baraka was elected secretary general. (Exact election date from general knowledge.)

timeline.title: 2021 elections: 81 seats, back in government
timeline.description: The Istiqlal nearly doubled its seats to 81 (third place), won 5,600 communal seats, 17 Councillors seats and 4 regional presidencies (Casablanca-Settat, Fès-Meknès, Laâyoune-Sakia El Hamra, Dakhla-Oued Ed-Dahab), and joined the RNI-PAM-PI coalition with 4 ministers. Enaam Mayara was elected president of the House of Councillors.

timeline.title: 18th congress: Baraka re-elected
timeline.description: At the 18th congress in Bouznika (3,600 delegates, theme 'Renew the pact for the nation and the citizen'), Baraka was re-elected unanimously in the early hours of 28 April 2024 after Rachid Afilal withdrew.

timeline.title: Akhannouch II reshuffle: additional Istiqlal ministers
timeline.description: The reshuffle brought in Abdessamad Kayouh (Transport) and Abdeljabbar Rachidi (Solidarity) among others; press reports describe the new line-up as more generous to the coalition parties. (Per-party counts not retrieved.)

achievements.title: Manifesto of Independence and leadership of the independence movement
achievements.description: The party claims the 11 January 1944 Manifesto and the mobilisation that led to independence in 1956 as its founding achievement.
achievements.verification: Historians (Encyclopedia.com, Britannica) confirm the Istiqlal authored the Manifesto and was the main nationalist party; independence in 1956 also resulted from the Sultan's stance and exile (1953), armed resistance and international pressure. The Manifesto anniversary is a national holiday.

achievements.title: Winning the 2007 elections and heading government
achievements.description: First place in 2007 (52 seats) and the premiership of Abbas El Fassi (2007-2011).
achievements.verification: Confirmed by official results and appointment.

achievements.title: Electoral rebound and return to government
achievements.description: From 46 to 81 seats and four ministries in 2021; largest group in the House of Councillors in 2015.
achievements.verification: Confirmed by Ministry of Interior results as reported by L'Opinion (party-owned) and Médias24 (independent).

achievements.title: Water policy under Nizar Baraka (dams, desalination, 'water highway')
achievements.description: The party credits its secretary general, as Minister of Equipment and Water, with the response to the 2022-2024 drought (dams, interconnection of basins, desalination plants).
achievements.verification: The National Programme for Drinking Water Supply and Irrigation 2020-2027 is a royal/state programme predating the government; independent evaluations not retrieved in this session.
